title: Best Quotes (by chapter, with page numbers)
text:
Best Quotes from Advanced Nutrition
and Human Metabolism by Sareen S.

Chapter 1 | Quotes From Pages -54
1.Cells are the very essence of life. Cells may be
defined as the basic living, structural, and
functional units of the human body.
2.A chain is only as strong as its weakest link.
3.Considering the relationship between the normal
functioning of a typical cell and the health of the total
organism—the human being—brings to mind the old rule:
'A chain is only as strong as its weakest link.'
4.The fluidity of the membrane also appears to affect the
structure and function of the proteins embedded in the lipid
membrane.
5.Normal intracellular communication among all cellular
components is vital for cell activation and survival.
6.The cell is a dynamic structure that is constantly in motion,


adapting to signals from its environment to maintain
homeostasis.
7.Dietary changes can elicit the induction of enzymes
necessary to cope with the changing nutrient load.
Chapter 2 | Quotes From Pages -84
1.Nutrition is the science of nourishment.
2.The body needs six classes of nutrients: carbohydrate, lipid,
protein, vitamins, minerals, and water.
3.The digestive tract, approximately 16 feet in length,
includes organs that comprise the gastrointestinal (GI) tract
as well as certain accessory organs.
4.Digestion occurs in the digestive tract and, once complete,
yields nutrients ready for absorption and use by the body.
5.The mucosa, the innermost layer, is made of three
sublayers...
6.Gastric juice contains an abundance of hydrochloric acid
secreted from gastric parietal cells.
7.The small intestine is the main site for nutrient digestion
and absorption.


8.Digestive secretions include primarily enzymes, but also
hydrochloric acid important for gastric digestion, and
bicarbonate and bile important for digestion and absorption
in the intestine.
Chapter 3 | Quotes From Pages -132
1.The major source of energy fuel in the average
human diet is carbohydrate, supplying half or
more of the total caloric intake.
2.Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, or
substances that produce these compounds when
hydrolyzed.
3.The most abundant monosaccharide in nature—and
certainly the most important nutritionally—is the
six-carbon sugar glucose.
4.The major polysaccharides of interest in nutrition are
glycogen, found in certain animal tissues, and starch and
cellulose, both of plant origin.
5.Monosaccharides with more than three carbons have more
than one chiral center.


6.In summary, nearly all dietary starches and disaccharides
ultimately are hydrolyzed completely by specific
glycosidases to their constituent monosaccharide units.
7.The pentose phosphate pathway generates important
intermediates not produced in other pathways.
8.Gluconeogenesis essentially reverses the glycolytic
pathway.
9.An increase in glucose-6-P is needed to activate the
gluconeogenesis pathway.
10.The Cori cycle describes the liver’s uptake and
gluconeogenic conversion of muscle-produced lactate to
glucose.




Chapter 4 | Quotes From Pages -158
1.Today, soluble and insoluble fibers may be
extracted or, in some cases, manufactured in
laboratories and added as an ingredient to create
foods that contain what we now call functional
fiber.
2.Examining these many components and their various
distinctive characteristics emphasizes the fact that dietary
fiber cannot be considered a single entity.
3.Diets rich in fiber are beneficial to varying degrees in the
prevention and/or management of several health problems.
4.Consumption of plant foods provides fiber in the diet. The
plant species, the part of the plant (leaf, root, stem), and the
plant’s maturity all influence the composition of the fiber
that is consumed.
5.The ability of some fibers to lower serum cholesterol
concentrations is based on a couple of events.
Chapter 5 | Quotes From Pages -204
1.The properTy ThaT seTs lipids apart from other


major nutrients is their solubility in organic
solvents such as ether, chloroform, and ace- tone.
2.Among the many compounds classified as lipids, only a
small number are important as dietary energy sources or as
functional or structural constituents within the cell.
3.Essential Fatty Acids If fat is entirely excluded from the
diet of humans, a con- dition develops that is characterized
by retarded growth, dermatitis, kidney lesions, and early
death.
4.The major sites for the formation of lipoproteins are the
intestine, which produces them from diet-derived lipids,
and the liver, which forms lipoproteins from endogenous
lipids.
5.Reverse cholesterol transport benefits the cardiovascular
system by reducing the amount of deposited cholesterol in
the vascular endothelium, and thus the risk of fatty plaque
formation and atherosclerosis.
6.Inflammation is just one part of the body’s innate immune
response to tissue damage or a foreign object.


Chapter 6 | Quotes From Pages -270
1.The importance of protein in nutrition and health
cannot be over-emphasized. It is quite appropriate
that the Greek word chosen as a name for this
nutrient is proteos, meaning “primary” or “taking
first place.
2.A dispensable amino acid may become indispensable if an
organ fails to function properly.
3.Adequate protein intake is recommended especially with
aging to combat muscle loss.
4.A complete protein contains all the indispensable amino
acids in the approximate amounts needed by humans.
Sources of complete proteins are mostly foods of animal
origin such as milk, yogurt, cheese, eggs, meat, fish, and
poultry.
5.Protein and amino acid requirements of humans are
influenced by age, body size, and physiological state, as
well as by the level of energy intake.
6.Not all creatinine, however, gets excreted in the urine.


Small amounts may be secreted into the gut and, like urea,
metabolized by bacteria in the intestine.
7.Protein deficiency can occur in those ingesting inadequate
protein with or without adequate energy.
8.The majority of proline synthesis is thought to occur
through intestinal cell glutamate metabolism.




Chapter 7 | Quotes From Pages -296
1.Integration of the metabolic processes, as outlined
in the preceding sections, allows the ‘constancy of
the internal milieu’ of humans and other
multicellular organisms that was described by the
French physiologist Claude Bernard over a
century ago.
2.The dynamics of substrate use in supplying energy for
physical exercise provide a practical example of how the
various metabolic pathways interrelate.
3.Energy homeostasis is maintained by regulation through
protein kinases.
4.One of the consequences of this enzymatic phosphorylation
is the reduction of lipolysis rather than direct carbohydrate
lipogenesis.
5.Muscle glycogen levels are the single most consistently
observed factor that contributes to fatigue.
6.Reversal of MetS means that the individual is no longer
classified as having the syndrome, and that some of the


signs of inflammation are also reduced.
7.The effectiveness of changing diet, lifestyle, and exercise
patterns in decreasing mortality and morbidity in people
with metabolic syndrome as they age will be an active area
of research and practice for the future.
Chapter 8 | Quotes From Pages -328
1.Recognition of body weight as an indicator of
health status is probably universal and as old as
humanity itself.
2.The prevalence of obesity has been observed throughout
history, but recently it has reached epidemic proportions.
3.Understanding the influences of genetics and hormones
that regulate our appetite, weight, and body composition
will assist in developing and implementing interventions.
4.Body weight is a good proxy in the nonathletic population,
and a low body weight may indicate malnutrition or an
eating disorder.
5.Weight loss or control of body weight becomes the
overriding goal in life, especially during stressful periods


when pressures become overwhelming.
6.Anorexia nervosa is a chronic, relapsing illness for many
individuals. Of the many psychiatric disorders, anorexia
nervosa possesses the highest mortality rate.
7.Leptin is a hormone secreted by white adipose tissue that
interacts with the hypothalamus to reduce hunger.
8.Binge eating is marked by a sense of lack of control over
eating during the binge episode.
9.The female athlete triad is described as a complex
interrelationship between menstrual status, bone health, and
energy availability.
10.The goals for the patient’s health are established, often
with a written contract signed by the patient as well as by
members of the health care team.
Chapter 9 | Quotes From Pages -392
1.The early part of the 20th century was the most
exciting era in the history of nutrition science.
2.Unfortu- nately, relating the function of the vitamin
directly to its deficiency syndrome is often impossible.


3.In a country with an abundant and varied food supply such
as the United States, the nutrition professional should think
in terms of what a specific vitamin does rather than what
disease it prevents.
4.Experimental research designs enable the investigator to
control or manipulate one or more variables...
5.Vitamin B12 undergoes little to no degradation prior to
excretion.
6.Vitamin B6 deficiency is relatively rare in the United
States.
7.Folate deficiency results in megaloblastic macrocytic
anemia—the release into circulation of red blood cells that
are fewer than normal in number as well as large and
immature.
8.The metabolic activities of various vitamins emphasize the
interconnectedness of nutrients in our bodies.
9.The presence of nitrogen-fixing bacteria in the plant root
nodules.
10.This statement reflects a time of groundbreaking


discoveries in nutrition, particularly concerning vitamins.




Chapter 10 | Quotes From Pages -446
1.Vitamin A is recognized as being essential for
vision as well as for cellular differentiation,
growth, reproduction, bone development, and
immune system functions.
2.The presence of vitamin E within the enterocyte is thought
to protect ²-carotene from oxidation; how
too high a concentration, vitamin E may inhibit carotenoid
absorption.
3.Calcium may be absorbed in the intestine by paracellular
transport that is also regulated in part by vitamin D.
4.Vitamin A, as retinoic acid, is needed by many cells for
differentiation, the process by which an immature cell is
transformed into a specific type of mature cell.
5.Vitamin K was named after the Danish word koagulation,
which means “coagulation.
6.Deficiency of vitamin D is widespread across the United
States and world.
Chapter 11 | Quotes From Pages -476


1.The importance of minerals in normal nutrition
and metabolism cannot be overstated, despite the
fact that they constitute only about 4% of total
body weight.
2.Calcium is the most abundant divalent cation in the body,
representing about 40% of the body’s mineral mass and
1.5% to 2% of total body weight.
3.The best food sources of calcium include dairy products,
especially milk, cheese, and yogurt, and selected seafood,
such as salmon and sardines.
4.Inadequate calcium intake, poor calcium absorption,
excessive calcium losses, or some combination of these
factors contribute to calcium deficiency.
5.The processes of calcification and mineralization of the
bone matrix has yet to be clearly delineated.
6.Osteoporosis affects both cortical and trabecular bone,
although trabecular bone has a higher turnover rate and is
affected to a greater extent than is cortical bone.
7.Calcium supplementation of 2 or 3 g daily also may


decrease chenodeoxycholate concentrations in bile and the
lithocholate:deoxycholate ratio in the feces.
Chapter 12 | Quotes From Pages -502
1.Despite the great diversity of specialized cellular
functions, the composition of the body fluids (the
internal environment) enveloping the cells remains
relatively constant under normal conditions.
2.This constant composition, or homeostasis, of the internal
environment is necessary for optimal activity of the cells.
3.Many minor disturbances inevitably occur in water
distribution, electrolyte balance, and pH of the body fluids
during metabolism.
4.The regulation of extracellular water osmolarity and
volume is largely the responsibility of the hypothalamus,
the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, and the kidneys.
5.Theoretical osmotic pressure presupposes that the solute
particles are unable to pass freely through the membrane.
6.When filtration pressure is negative, a net reabsorption of
water from the ISF to the plasma occurs.


7.The removal of potentially toxic waste products, a major
function of the kidneys, is accomplished through the
formation of urine.
8.Normal physiological function depends upon proper
control of the body fluid acid–base balance.
9.Elevations (even in the normal range) in plasma sodium
concentrations appear to be associated with arterial
thickening and narrowing and impaired endothelial cell
elasticity, factors that increase blood pressure.
10.High potassium intake is also known to affect blood
pressure—but inversely.




Chapter 13 | Quotes From Pages -568
1.The trace minerals or trace elements (also called
microminerals) initially gained the description
'trace' because their concentrations in tissue were
not easily quantified by early analytical methods.
2.... trace minerals can be analyzed by a variety of
techniques.
3.Trace minerals are now typically defined as minerals that
are needed by the body in small amounts, that is, less than
100 mg per day.
4.However, some of the trace elements may be categorized as
ultratrace if required in amounts of less than 1 mg per day.
5.Chapter 13 describes the sources, digestion, absorption,
transport, storage, functions, interactions with other
nutrients, excretion, recommended intakes, deficiency,
toxicity, and assessment of nutrient for the trace minerals
iron, zinc, and copper, and the ultratrace minerals selenium,
iodine, and molybdenum.
6.Interestingly, although selenocysteine is required for


selenium-dependent enzyme function, selenocysteine
obtained directly from the diet or selenomethionine
degradation cannot be utilized.
7.The multiple effects of the thyroid hormones result from
the hormones’ occupancy of nuclear receptors, with
subsequent effects on gene expression.
8.Selenium deficiency occurs primarily in selected regions of
the world such as China, central Africa, and parts of
Europe.
Chapter 14 | Quotes From Pages -584
1.Most Americans obtain the majority of dietary
fluoride from drinking water, which provides
about 0.24 mg of fluoride/cup.
2.Fluoride deficiency in test animals has been reported to
result in curtailed growth, infertility, and anemia.
3.Arsenic appears to facilitate the body’s use of methyl
groups, such as S-adenosylmethionine (SAM).
4.Boron promotes health but has not been shown to have
clear biochemical functions in humans.
